newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leadership candidate pledges conservative rule.
newsitem.headline: HK leadership candidate pledges conservative rule.

text.p: A leading candidate for Hong Kong's 1997 post-colonial leadership said in an interview published on Tuesday he would avoid making drastic changes and would aim for a conservative style of rule.

"If I were to become Chief Executive, I'm at the head of a moderate, relatively conservative government," Sir Ti Liang Yang, Hong Kong's former chief justice, told the English-language daily South China Morning Post.
"I don't want to see more great challenges or great reforms over the initial couple of years after 1997," Yang said.

In an opinion poll published on the weekend Yang emerged as the front-runner among candidates who have declared an interest in governing Hong Kong after Britain hands the capitalist territory of 6.3 million people back to China at midnight next June 30.

Hong Kong's future leader will not be elected, but selected by a China-controlled committee next month. The public opinion poll gave Yang 45 percent support, ahead of second-placed shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa's 24 percent.

"There have been a lot of changes and debate over the last few years. I think people want a period to consolidate what we've gained, time to think about the future and a period of quiet to reassess ourselves," Yang said.
"The change of sovereignty is a big enough change. We need to psychologically adjust ourselves," he said.

"I envisage a Hong Kong which is very much the same as the Hong Kong we used to know," Yang said, an apparent reference to the period before colonial Governor Chris Patten, who arrived in 1992, introduced a more democratic electoral system.

When Britain withdraws, Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region of communist-ruled China. Autonomy is promised by Beijing under the Sino-British handover treaty, but many in Hong Kong fear that in reality Beijing will meddle.
Yang said he would "consolidate and fine-tune" present Hong Kong policies including those on welfare, housing and human rights, but without taking any "daring reform measures", the newspaper said.

China has criticised Hong Kong and Patten for boosting welfare spending and for bringing in a Bill of Rights which Beijing says it will dilute after the handover next year. Last year Yang echoed China's criticisms.

China has also vowed to dismantle Hong Kong's fully elected Legislative Council and appoint a new "provisional legislature" in retaliation for Patten's moves to expand democracy in the territory against Beijing's will.

Yang said he would disappoint some groups such as the Democratic Party, the largest party in the legislature, over their calls for a faster pace of democratisation, but he said full democracy was nonetheless a distant goal.
"Universal suffrage must be the ultimate aim. I don't think any Chief Executive can say when...One's got to see how the situation develops," Yang said.
He said the introduction of democracy should happen in a gradual and orderly manner as laid down in the Basic Law, Hong Kong's post-handover constitution promulgated by China.
